items.content:
In a review of our cybersecurity evaluations, we found three incidents in which a Claude model reached the internet from within or while interacting with a third-party evaluation environment, and then gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations.

Our post describes what happened, how it happened, and what we’re changing. We encourage other AI developers to perform similar reviews.

We conducted this review together with @Irregular, one of our evaluation partners, and thank them for the joint investigation and their collaboration on this post. This type of collaboration is increasingly critical to safe, rigorous evaluation of models, and we look forward to continuing to work together on security.

Today...
items.content:
For decades, we’ve dreamed of robots that can seamlessly step into our world and lend a hand.

Today, we take a major stride toward making that dream a reality:

Introducing Gemini Robotics 2 from @GoogleDeepMind, the intelligence layer powering the next generation of truly adaptable robots. This major advance unlocks intelligent whole-body control, advanced dexterity, and even multi-robot collaboration 🤯.

Ok but... how does a robot actually "think"?

Real-world tasks take time and planning. To manage that complexity, our new embodied reasoning model, Gemini Robotics ER 2, acts as the robot’s high-level brain, enhancing the robot’s capabilities to:

— Observe the environment
— Reason about the actions needed to complete the task
— Coordinate with the vision-language-action model to carry out actions
— Track progress until the job is done

This setup allows robots to execute complex multi-step workflows, self-correct if a step fails, and adapt to completely novel situations.

Learn more about Gemini Robotics ER 2 (and our two other brand new models) here: https://t.co/1YEpoYAhww

1. Not okay: harne...
items.content:
Quick reminder of what's ok vs not ok with harnesses used for playing ARC-AGI-3:

1. Not okay: harnesses that were custom-made to solve the benchmark or that contain knowledge about the benchmark format / contents.

2. Fine: general-purpose API settings that were not developed for ARC-AGI-3 and that are available to all API users.

In the past, we've had a lot of back and forth with OpenAI about how to best test their models, especially with regard to compaction. I'm glad they're starting to figure out the answer.

Of course, if each provider uses different settings when getting their model tested, it creates a potential parity issue. My take is that this is fine as long as the settings and the cost are clearly reported.

items.content:
Today @fireship_dev covered this:

- Indie hackers may be the first type of developer to go extinct

- The classic indie hacking playbook (last decade): learn to code → find a niche → ship a micro-SaaS → build in public → post MRR screenshots after failures → repeat until it works

- Coding used to be hard and expensive, so execution mattered far more than ideas

- That equation has flipped: execution now costs ~$20/month, so anyone can build personal software instead of paying for SaaS

- Example: Why pay $29/month for a product when Claude Code can recreate a better version in 20 minutes?  

- Building in public on X makes it easy for others to steal your idea/roadmap

- AI raises the ceiling (indie hackers become far more productive) but also lowers the floor (the space is now crowded with normies who can vibe-code their own tools)

@mkratsios47 @NSF @RapidResponse47 @WHOSTP47 @teamuidp The amount of basic research done in industry is nowhere near the amount done in universities. 
At various times, there have been industry labs that had fundamental research activities and have made important scientific contributions. 
Examples in information technology include Bell Labs, IBM Research, Xerox PARC, GE, Phillips, NEC, and several other. That disappeared in the 1990s.
Microsoft Research picked up the torch in the 2000s, followed (to some extent) by Google and then Meta (for about a decade until recently).
But their innovations almost always built on top of academic work, and certainly profited from the whole research ecosystem.

items.title:

There's been an explosion of interest in model routing - you don't a...
items.content:
Introducing the Parse Gateway 

There's been an explosion of interest in model routing - you don't always need the best model for every task.

That is especially true for document parsing 📄🔀:
- Some pages are text-heavy and relatively simple. These pages can be handled by cheap, fast text-based parsers
- Other pages are more complex with a variety of dimensions: scans, dense tables, complex diagrams and charts, garbled binary text, and more. 

The trick is to use a good parse router that can optimize the parsing mode depending on page complexity! 

The Parse Gateway is based on the `is_complex` functionality we introduced within liteparse, which estimates the complexity of a page at the page level. Depending on the complexity, it routes the page to our various modes within LlamaParse: cost-effective, agentic, and agentic plus. 

The gateway code itself is open-source, but you can also directly find an implementation within our MCP server 

Check out the blog! https://t.co/ovsIN1TOYD

LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8

items.content:
@mkratsios47 @NSF @RapidResponse47 @WHOSTP47 @teamuidp The main rationale for PhD students to be affiliated with industry is access to heavy equipment unavailable in academia. 
For AI research, it's access to compute. 

But one has to be careful that the kind of creative exploration that is enabled by academic research environments is not stunted by industry environments that are often much more goal oriented. 

France has had a government-sponsored program called CIFRE for over 40 years that allows PhD students to spend 20% to 80% of their time as residents in an industry lab (FAIR-Paris has been graduating a dozen of those per year for the last decade).
There are provisions to allow students to do actual research and to publish, and to prevent them from being used as cheap engineers.

items.title: Thinking Machines' new Inkling Small scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within...
items.content:
Thinking Machines' new Inkling Small scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within a point of its flagship sibling Inkling with less than a third of the total and active parameters

Inkling Small is @thinkymachines second model release, arriving two weeks after Inkling launched at 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Thinking Machines is the San Francisco-based AI lab founded by former @OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window.

Key results:

➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active.

➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%).

➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%).

➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling.

Additional model details:

➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model (Apache 2.0 license)

➤ Size: 276B total parameters, 12B active (MoE)

➤ Input modalities: Text, image, and speech

➤ Output modalities: Text

➤ Context window: 256K tokens (Inkling supports 1M)

Congratulations to the team at Thinking Machines on the release!

items.content_html:
@npparikh @story645 France has had a industry-resident PhD program called CIFRE for over 4 decades.

It's good, but there are guardrails to guarantee that students can do actual research and publish their work, and to prevent the hosting industry from using them as cheap engineering labor.

FAIR-Paris has graduated about a dozen PhD students per year for the last decade (in collaboration with their academic institution). Incredibly successful and productive program.

✅ Create higher reliability and code maintainability, since you no longer have to create your own async service that hits our API for every file.

items.content:
Before asking what your agents can automate, leaders should ask whether the infrastructure beneath them can support it at scale.

82% of organizations had unknown agents operating in their environments. 65% had already experienced agent-related security incidents.

Agent governance cannot live inside a prompt. It must sit below the agent — inside secure runtimes, centralized policy controls, and continuous observability layers.

What would your AI production strategy look like under real enterprise pressure?

Check out the full article: https://t.co/8x9gFa6BrH

The real story is that most enterprise architec...
items.content:
The real story is not that AI pilots are expensive.

The real story is that most enterprise architectures were designed for demonstration — not for the continuous loops that production agents actually run.

A chatbot request costs cents. An agentic task consuming context, memory, retrieval, tool calls, and inference at scale can generate approximately $1.4 million in annual cloud costs from just 1,000 agent tasks per day.

Pilots pulse. Production loops — and most architectures were never built for the difference.

items.content:
Here is how production AI infrastructure actually layers together:

Data must be governed, contextualized, and available at the speed agents require. Metadata, lineage, access policies, and high-throughput pipelines determine whether enterprise information becomes reliable context — or an expensive bottleneck.

Networking must be designed for GPU communication patterns, low latency, and minimal congestion. NVIDIA addresses this with NVIDIA AI networking platforms that keep GPUs constantly fed with data, so expensive GPUs do not sit idle and cluster traffic moves with the low latency accelerated workloads require.

Compute placement must match performance, sovereignty, latency, and economics. Siemens Energy's move to an HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA private cloud, delivered through HPE GreenLake, illustrates what the full HPE and NVIDIA stack delivers for demanding engineering workloads.

HPE and NVIDIA are collaborating to deliver HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA enterprise reference architectures — compute, networking, storage, software, and governance in enterprise reference architectures — so enterprises can move from fragile pilots to repeatable operations.

Security in agentic AI is a different problem than traditional IT security.

@HPE's approach with @NVIDIA's NeMo architecture:

→ Certified skill catalogs: every MCP tool is vetted before deployment
→ Agents never hold passwords, credentials are issued per-task, then revoked
→ Agent-level sandboxing so you can reset one agent without taking down the whole system

Granular control. Not kill-switch control.

items.content:
This is not only a problem for tech companies.

Consider hospitals running clinical decision agents. Manufacturers operating predictive maintenance loops. Logistics hubs routing shipments through autonomous models. Financial services firms processing compliance workflows with no human in the loop.

Every one of these environments faces the same underlying challenge:

→ Data that is not governed at agent speed

→ Networks not designed for GPU communication patterns

→ Workloads placed on cost assumptions built for pilots, not persistence

→ Governance designed for the prompt layer — not the infrastructure layer 

HPE and NVIDIA are addressing these gaps through HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA enterprise reference architectures built for production scale. The architecture gap is not theoretical. It is operational.

→ A runtime environment (@HPE uses @NVIDIA's OpenShell, Kubernetes-based)
→ Model inferencing, ideally on the same box
→ Fast, persistent memory the agent can read and write continuously

Miss any one of these and it becomes much harder to build a true agentic system. Instead, you may end up with something closer to an expensive chatbot.

items.title:
More data can make decisions slower, not smarter, because teams keep searching for certainty.

When ...
items.content:
More data can make decisions slower, not smarter, because teams keep searching for certainty.

When every new signal opens another discussion, action is delayed even after enough evidence is already available.

The problem is not data abundance.

Microblog @antgrasso #SmartData

The problem starts when every new dataset creates another option to evaluate, another meeting to align, or another reason to delay execution.

In data-rich environments, leaders need clear thresholds for when information is sufficient and ownership is assigned.

Without that discipline, decisions are revisited instead of executed, and activity replaces progress.

This is why I have discussed smart data several times in previous posts.

Better decisions need data that is relevant, reliable, and ready to support action, not just more information to process.

items.title: NVIDIA's Cosmos3-Super-4Step distills are the new #1 open weights model for Image to Video and #3 fo...
items.content:
NVIDIA's Cosmos3-Super-4Step distills are the new #1 open weights model for Image to Video and #3 for Text to Image in the Artificial Analysis Arena

Cosmos3-Super-Text2Image-4Step and Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video-4Step are distilled variants of NVIDIA's 64B Cosmos3-Super world foundation model, released with open weights on July 20. NVIDIA’s distillation has cut inference from 50 steps (Text to Image) and 35 steps (Image to Video) down to just 4, and removed the need for classifier-free guidance. NVIDIA positions the Cosmos 3 family as world foundation models for physical AI, generating training data and video for robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial systems, with output up to 720p and Image to Video clips of ~8 seconds (189 frames at 24 FPS) by default.

In the Artificial Analysis Arenas, Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video-4Step is the new #1 open weights model on our Image to Video Leaderboard, and #15 overall, ahead of the full 35-step Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video. Cosmos3-Super-Text2Image-4Step ranks #3 among open weights models on our Text to Image Leaderboard, and #25 overall.

Both models are available now on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW-1.1 license, which permits commercial use.

Congratulations to @NVIDIAAI on the release!

See below for comparisons between the Cosmos3-Super 4Step models and other leading models in the Artificial Analysis Image and Video Arenas 🧵

items.title:
What does it take to run Kimi K3 locally? (it unfortunately isn’t going to run on your MacBook)

Kim...
items.content:
What does it take to run Kimi K3 locally? (it unfortunately isn’t going to run on your MacBook)

Kimi K3 requires ~1.56 TB of memory for its weights alone, and the only current single-node systems that meet this bar (while supporting 4-bit precision) are NVIDIA’s B300 and AMD’s MI350X/MI355X. Unlike most earlier open-weights models, Kimi K3 is too large to run on any single Hopper, B200 or MI300X node.

Key takeaways when running Kimi K3 locally:

➤ It has 2.8 trillion total parameters, making it the largest open-weights model ever released

➤ Its hybrid attention mechanism reduces the amount of KV cache space required per token. For example, at 256K context on a GB300 NVL72, Kimi K3 could theoretically support over 2,000 concurrent requests using a 16-bit KV cache, compared to ~1,000 for Kimi K2.6 (when disregarding the throughput roofline)

➤ In total, running Kimi K3 locally while using its full 1M context window would require ~1.59 TB of memory for one user, growing by ~30 GB per additional concurrent user if using 16-bit KV cache

➤ The high memory requirement leads to a total system cost in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, highly dependent on specific hardware configuration and volume-based pricing

➤ The above points do not consider serving speed, which adds an additional layer of complexity - it is considerably more difficult to serve at a reasonable speed at high concurrency, vs. simply fitting the model inside available memory

Realistic hardware configurations that can both fit Kimi K3’s weights and leave room for KV cache include:

➤ NVIDIA: 8x B300 or GB300; 16x B200 or GB200 (GB chips as part of an NVL72 rack)

➤ AMD: 8x MI350X or MI355X

We will be publishing day-1 inference benchmarking results for Kimi K3 on a subset of capable hardware shortly, and will track how serving performance improves as inference stacks mature.

items.title: A screen-free box that trades WhatsApp voice notes with the grandparents went viral this week, and t...
items.content:
A screen-free box that trades WhatsApp voice notes with the grandparents went viral this week, and the build story makes it even cooler.

Dan Peguine asked Claude Fable for a manual. It generated an illustrated, kid-readable guide with a single prompt.

The hardware: a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 "smaller than a chocolate bar," a USB speaker and mic, and two big buttons as the only controls.

The box joins WhatsApp with its own phone number, so only messages meant for the kids reach their room. Grandparents get a headphones-emoji "listened" receipt when the children play their message.

He built it with his son, iterating on the UX for a few weeks. The Fable manual lists the child as Chief Engineer.

Peguine: "I love that they are in direct contact without me in the middle and without screens."

You can just build things!

1. Processed food in the U.S. is engineered to make you fat and keep y...
items.content:
About food and staying lean:

1. Processed food in the U.S. is engineered to make you fat and keep you coming back for more.

2. If most of your food comes from the center aisles of the grocery store, especially from eye-level shelves, you're eating garbage.

3. Drinks at most fast-food restaurants are poison. Very common to find drinks with 150+ grams of sugar. Instead of buying a drink, buy a blender.

4. Everyone I know who started keto, paleo, Atkins, or a similar diet quit after a few weeks, regained all their weight back, and then some. Diets don't work.

5. You don't need to cut out entire food groups to stay lean. Don't listen to people who say you shouldn't eat carbohydrates or fats.

6. Staying lean isn't as simple as "calories in versus calories out." Calories matter. Protein and fiber make staying lean dramatically easier.

7. You can get fat eating healthy food. Healthy and non-caloric foods aren't the same. Olive oil is good for you, but it's also very caloric.

8. The closer you can get to regularly eating a plate made of single-ingredient foods, the better off you are.

9. It's very hard to overeat fruits and vegetables.

10. Walk and sleep more.
